transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-24
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Participants: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Lena Cho (CTO, Skyport), Markus Engel (ML Engineer), Priya Nair (Infra Lead)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Discussed migration off OpenAI and in-house vLLM/TGI to Redwood. Focus on performance parity, private deployment options, and security requirements. Next steps: share security pack, propose benchmark plan, schedule eval.

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro from our side, I'm Samira, AE at Redwood, and Diego is our systems engineer who will dig into the technical bits. how about you folks?
[00:12] Lena: Hi all, Lena here, CTO at Skyport Systems. We're running a mix of OpenAI hosted + a homegrown vLLM/TGI inference layer for lower latency.
[00:20] Markus: Markus - I own the model infra, have been tinkering with vLLM, TGI stack, and some int8 quant flows.
[00:26] Priya: Priya, infra lead. I'm focused on network/VPC, peering, KMS and compliance.
[00:32] Samira: Great. high level — you're evaluating Redwood to consolidate serving across hosted, dedicated or private. Can you share what the biggest pain points are today?
[00:40] Lena: Yeah, it's really two things: cost unpredictability on OpenAI at scale, and ops overhead keeping vLLM/TGI clusters healthy. also parity — we need to ensure outputs match or are at least within acceptable drift.
[00:52] Diego: When you say parity, are you referring to token-level output comparability, or downstream metric parity (NLP task scores)?
[00:58] Markus: both. For search relevance reranking we need same top-k ordering, for assistants the instruction-following behavior should be consistent. small word swaps are okay but not large regression.
[01:10] Samira: That makes sense. On the parity front we typically run side-by-side evals with your prompt set — we can do end-to-end scoring. Also note Redwood supports model variants and quant profiles so we can match cost/latency tradeoffs.
[01:24] Priya: Our compliance reqs: SOC2, SSO/SAML, fine-grained RBAC, KMS integration and audit logs. For private deployment we need HSM-backed keys and VPC peering — is that supported?
[01:34] Diego: Yes on those. Private mode includes customer-managed KMS integration and audit logs. HSM integrations are possible via our enterprise package. VPC peering and private control plane are supported; we do catalog the exact network flows in the security pack I'll send.
[01:46] Lena: How much effort is it to move models? our models are in TGI/vLLM artifacts, plus we use a lot of prefix KV cache in vLLM for chat history speedups.
[02:00] Diego: We ingest standard model artifacts (HF format, GGUF variants) and have adapters for vLLM/TGI checkpoints in many cases. KV cache semantics can be preserved — we support prefix caching and KV reuse patterns. there's sometimes conversion steps for optimized kernels but it's automated in our onboarding tooling.
[02:16] Markus: conversion steps like quantization or kernel mapping — do those change generation behavior?
[02:22] Diego: They can. quantization (4-bit, int8) may introduce small distributional changes. we run regression evals and you can pin to float or int8 profiles until you're comfortable. also we have rolling rollout and can fallback to a higher-precision variant if quality drops.
[02:38] Samira: to follow up — typical plan is: 1) exchange prompt sets and eval metrics; 2) run side-by-side benchmarks (latency, throughput, quality) on a dedicated pool; 3) assess private deploy if network/security needs require it.
[02:52] Lena: Sounds good. latency is critical for us — p95 sub-120ms on a 512-token seq is our target for assistant flows, and reranking needs p99 under 60ms for short contexts.
[03:06] Markus: Also concurrency patterns: many short requests vs fewer long ones — batching strategy matters.
[03:12] Diego: Right, Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching and smart routing. you can configure latency SLOs and cost budgets, and runtime will route to lower-cost batched backends for less latency-sensitive traffic. there's also automatic prefix caching which helps in assistant scenarios.
[03:28] Priya: For private deployment, how does autoscaling work? we have burst patterns at end of month, can't have cold-start spikes.
[03:36] Diego: Dedicated pools have configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity. for private on-prem we offer a control plane that triggers scale-up via your orchestrator; there's a warm pool option to keep instance state for rapid scale.
[03:50] Lena: Any public numbers you can share on throughput per GPU vs vLLM? our infra folks optimized kernels for our weight-dtypes so we're curious about comparisons.
[04:00] Samira: We have benchmark decks — I'll share them — but results vary by model, hardware, and sequence distribution. Diego can propose a bench that mirrors your profile.
[04:10] Diego: For context, we optimize kernel selection per model/seq-length. with quantized runtimes we generally see 1.5–3x throughput gains vs unoptimized FP16 for some LLMs, but that depends. We can instrument KV cache hit rates too which impacts per-token cost.
[04:28] Markus: When you mention instrumenting KV cache hit rates — can we get token-level cost breakdowns? that's important for our finance team.
[04:34] Samira: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdowns per model/route, and you can export for chargeback.
[04:42] Priya: On networking: we require VPC peering, restricted egress, and detailed flow logs for audits. Can Redwood Private be air-gapped?
[04:52] Diego: We have an on-prem package for regulated customers that can be air-gapped. more commonly customers use VPC private mode with a customer-managed control plane. I'll include network diagrams in the security pack.
[05:04] Lena: What's the lift for SSO/SAML and provisioning? we want SCIM to provision role-based access.
[05:10] Samira: SSO/SAML and SCIM are supported. RBAC is configurable in the Console and can be mapped to your IdP groups.
[05:18] Markus: Let's dive into parity concerns — we've seen small token shifts when moving from OpenAI to other runtimes. do you have examples of where behavior shifted unexpectedly?
[05:28] Diego: Yes — usually from tokenization differences or beam sampling/order of token generation when kernels differ. We do a token-level diff and downstream metric checks. In a few past cases we recommended minor prompt templating tweaks or pinned a model variant.
[05:40] Lena: For our side, we can tolerate minor wording differences but not functional regressions. who owns the regression triage during the eval?
[05:48] Samira: Diego's team will lead technical triage with you. Redwood can run regression alerts tied to your eval prompts and will notify on any drop in chosen metrics.
[05:56] Markus: About input/output formats — we rely heavily on structured tool calling and function outputs, and some of our tool chains expect precise JSON schemas. Does Redwood support tool/call structured outputs?
[06:08] Diego: Yes — function calling and structured output are supported. We also have post-processing hooks to validate JSON schemas and will report schema mismatches in logs.
[06:18] Priya: Billing model — we need predictable unit economics. Hosted per-token pricing is fine, but for scale we want committed Dedicated with monthly commit. what's Redwood's dedicated pricing model?
[06:28] Samira: Dedicated is reserved capacity — monthly/annual commits. you get predictable throughput and discounts versus hosted. We'll surface example pricing based on your traffic profile in the proposal.
[06:36] Lena: If we start hosted then move to private later, how much rework is expected?
[06:40] Diego: We designed the API and config to be consistent - same code can point to hosted or private endpoints. Model versioning and rollout policies transfer. The main work is network and key management for Private. Data residency and audit configuration is extra but we help with runbooks.
[06:56] Markus: For the benchmark, can you run against our in-house vLLM optimized artifacts? we want to compare the same compiled weights.
[07:04] Diego: We'll take your artifacts and either run them as-is where supported or convert to an optimized runtime. we record differences for you. If you want absolute parity we can run both on vLLM and on Redwood with identical seeds and sampling settings to compare.
[07:18] Samira: On timeline — what are you aiming for?
[07:22] Lena: Ideally a pilot within 2–3 weeks, then decide by end of next quarter. we have exec pressure to reduce costs.
[07:30] Samira: Good — we can probably start a 1-week dedicated eval in that window.
[07:34] Priya: A few more security specifics — do you support customer-managed encryption keys that never leave our cloud tenant?
[07:42] Diego: Yes, we support KMS integration and HSM options where keys can be customer-controlled. for hosted customers there are envelope encryption patterns; for private we can do direct KMS/HSM control.
[07:54] Markus: You mentioned fallbacks — if a model variant regresses in quality, what's the automated fallback approach?
[08:00] Diego: We support rollout policies with automatic fallback to a pinned model or a higher-tier hosted variant. There's also region routing if a capacity issue occurs.
[08:08] Lena: Any data residency constraints we should be aware of?
[08:12] Samira: We support region pinning and private deployments to meet residency.
[08:16] Priya: For the eval, what telemetry will you require from our side?
[08:20] Diego: We'll ask for: sample prompts, latency SLOs, throughput targets, and a baseline of current p50/p95/p99. we'll also ask for a few hundred annotated examples for quality checks.
[08:32] Markus: On cost, can you provide a token-level cost projection broken into compute, storage (KV), and network?
[08:38] Samira: Yes — Redwood Optimize gives recommendations and a cost breakdown. we'll do a sample model-cost calc for your traffic profile.
[08:46] Lena: What about model updates and version pinning? our release cadence is weekly.
[08:50] Diego: You can pin model versions and use canary rollouts or A/B tests. rollout hooks let you do gradual traffic shifting and automatic rollback on metric drops.
[08:58] Priya: Operationally, in Private mode who will manage runtime updates and security patches?
[09:04] Samira: There's an ops model choice — Redwood can operate the control plane and push runtime updates, or we can hand over the control plane. For fully on-prem air-gapped you'd manage patches, but we provide update bundles and runbooks.
[09:16] Markus: Any difference in latency between hosted and private?
[09:20] Diego: Private in-region will often be equal or slightly better because of network proximity and pinned hardware. hosted introduces network hop but we have edge routing to reduce latency.
[09:30] Lena: Let's talk about the benchmark metrics you propose.
[09:32] Diego: We'll measure p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec throughput, token-cost, KV cache hit rate, and quality metrics you define. we'll run with identical seeds and sampling to avoid stochastic drift.
[09:46] Markus: How do you instrument model RNG seeds and sampling? we've seen different RNG implementations create variation.
[09:52] Diego: We can control sampling parameters and use deterministic sampling where possible; the runtime supports seed control and matching top-k/top-p settings. If there's undocumented RNG behaviour in upstream libs we note that in the diff.
[10:04] Samira: quick check — any legal/procurement blockers?
[10:08] Lena: Standard NDA is already in place. procurement will need standard vendor terms but nothing exceptional so far.
[10:14] Priya: We'll need liability limits and DPA — those are standard.
[10:18] Samira: Good, we'll include those in the security/contract packet.
[10:22] Markus: A nit — in-house we do prefix KV caching to avoid regen costs; can Redwood's caching be flushed and warmed deterministically during evaluation?
[10:32] Diego: Yes, you can seed the prefix cache before the run and we can control cache eviction or warm pools to ensure fair comparison.
[10:40] Lena: Suppose we hit a quality regression on a quantized profile. What's the expected turnaround for a fix?
[10:46] Diego: Usually a day or two to triage; sometimes it's a config change like different quant profile, sometimes code-level kernel tweak which could take longer. We'll prioritize regressions in the eval.
[10:58] Samira: For next steps, I'll send the security pack and a proposed timeline. Diego will send the benchmark plan. Markus will share prompts. anything else?
[11:08] Markus: Could you include cost scenarios for both hosted burst vs dedicated reserved capacity?
[11:12] Samira: Yep — included in the proposal.
[11:16] Priya: And network diagrams and required firewall rules.
[11:20] Diego: Will include.
[11:22] Lena: Thanks, this was helpful. we'll align internally and aim to turn around the prompt set by Thursday.
[11:28] Samira: Great. we'll target the eval the week of 2026-03-30. Thanks everyone.
[11:34] (end of recorded portion)
